title: The Bedroom Where Reginald Mengi Assembled His First Pens
dek: In Tanzania's shortages of the mid-1980s, a senior accountant who had been refused a bank loan began putting together Kenyan pen parts at home.

story.company: IPP (later IPP Group and IPP Media)
story.event: Assembling imported pen components in his bedroom after a bank refused him a loan
story.summary: During Tanzania's shortages of 1983 and 1984, Reginald Mengi, a senior accountant at Coopers & Lybrand, was refused a $4,000 loan by the National Bank of Commerce and instead arranged a consignment of pen components from Kenya, which he assembled in his bedroom in Dar es Salaam. He left the firm in October 1989 to run his own businesses, and in 1994 his IPP group launched The Guardian newspaper and the ITV television station with Radio One.
paragraphs: During the shortages of 1983 and 1984, a consignment of ballpoint-pen parts reached Dar es Salaam, and Reginald Mengi had nowhere to keep it. "When the components arrived I didn't know where to put them," he told Forbes Africa in 2014. He chose his bedroom, and that is where the assembly began.

Mengi was not a trader by training. A chartered accountant who had qualified in Britain, he returned to Tanzania in 1971 to join the accounting firm Coopers & Lybrand, where he rose to chairman and managing partner. From mid-1983, as he recalled in his memoir, the country was short of almost everything; the government was harassing and detaining traders it accused of hoarding. One profile says his first idea came on a day he tried to buy a pen and could not find one.

He decided to bring pens in from Kenya. The state-owned National Bank of Commerce turned down his request for a $4,000 loan, so he worked out an arrangement with business contacts across the border instead. The lorry carrying the parts from Mombasa broke down at the Horohoro border post, but the load got through. In his memoir he says he made his first million dollars within a year, a figure that rests on his own account.

He did not leave the firm straight away. Bonite Bottlers, his Coca-Cola plant in Moshi, was set up in 1987, and he went on to make shoe polish from charcoal and oil and a skin scrub from bottled sea mud. He left Coopers & Lybrand in October 1989. "Some people leave their jobs when things are bad, but I left mine when things were really good," he said later. The new life meant sixteen-hour days, a Peugeot 104 in place of a 504, and some deliveries made on foot.

After Tanzania opened its media to private owners in the early 1990s, he moved into another field he had no training in. His group launched The Guardian newspaper in 1994, and its station ITV began broadcasting, alongside Radio One, on 10 June that year. When he died in Dubai on 2 May 2019, aged 75, it was those two stations that confirmed the news.

quote.text: Even a good man sees evil days, as long as his good deed has not ripened; but when his good deed has ripened, then does the good man see happy days.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: The verse is about conduct, not profit, but it names a stretch every founder meets: the work is sound and the results have not arrived. Mengi's refused loan and stranded lorry belonged to that stretch, and a bedroom full of parts was what the time before ripening looked like.

reflection: Some mornings the evidence that you chose well is thin. A bank says no, a delivery stalls at a border, and the only place left for the work is a corner of the room you also need for sleep. Mengi's story does not prove that this stage always ends well; plenty of businesses started at home never ripen. What it shows is that the early stage tends to look like this even when it does.
You do not have to read every lean day as a verdict. It may simply be one of the days before the ripening, and it deserves food, sleep and a sensible finishing time like any other.
invitation: Tonight, when you stop, leave your working corner tidy enough to be part of your home again: close the laptop, put the papers in one pile, and let the space rest until morning.

sources.title: How Mengi ventured into business by starting small

research_notes: Episode: the slate named the move into media around 1993. No accessible source gives Mengi's own account of why or how he decided to start ITV or The Guardian (the only stated motive, letting fans watch the 1994 World Cup, comes from a single EastAfrican opinion column that was blocked), so the edition tells the better-documented pen-assembly start and mentions the media launch as what followed. Order of events: The Citizen's 2014 report of the Forbes Africa interview says his first idea came after he had quit PwC; the 2019 Citizen and EastAfrican articles, drawing on his memoir, say he started the pens while still at Coopers & Lybrand and decided to quit after they did well, and the EastAfrican dates his departure to October 1989. Bonite Bottlers (1987) also predates that departure, so the story follows the memoir and the 1989 date. Dates of the pen business: the memoir, as reported, places the shortages from mid-1983 (EastAfrican: mid-1983 to 1984) without a precise start date, so the story says 1983 and 1984. Media dates: The Citizen (2014) says The Guardian launched in 1994 and ITV 'a year later', calling ITV Tanzania's first television network; the Media Ownership Monitor gives ITV's registration as 17 January 1994 and its start as 10 June 1994, and Coastal Television Network is reported to have begun broadcasting earlier in 1994, so the story uses the Monitor's date and does not call ITV the first. Age: The EastAfrican and The National say he died aged 75 and the Monitor gives his birth year as 1944; The Citizen's 2019 article says 77. The story uses 75. Outcome figure: 'first million dollars within a year' comes only from his memoir as reported by The EastAfrican and is attributed to him. Independence: The Citizen and The EastAfrican both belong to Nation Media Group, and their 2019 articles share much of their wording, so the loan and lorry details rest effectively on one account drawn from the memoir; the 2014 Citizen piece is a separate report of the Forbes Africa interview. The original Forbes Africa and Forbes pieces and Mengi's own website did not load.
